### CYSO-MIKKOLA-2013-P122-123
- **Title / author / year:** *Owls of the World: A Photographic Guide* / Heimo Mikkola / 2013.

- **Pages:** diagnosis/morphology pp.298–301; measurements p.300; breeding/habitat pp.303–304.
- **Facts:** darkest/darker-grey taxon, heavy broad black streaking, coarse vermiculation, narrow bars and larger white spots; no rufous morph. Specimen wing means male n=10 153.3 mm, female n=13 153.5 mm; eggs Apr–May, chicks late Apr–Jul; villages/light woodland/open pine forest.

- **Stage/facts:** ancient olive grove; juvenile fed by an adult on 21 June; several fledged juveniles photographed on 27 June; at least two young fledged.
- **Limits/decision:** no hatch age, sex, controlled flight test or continuous sequence. Supports an age-unknown, branch-supported fledged juvenile only.

### CYSO-BIRDLIFE-CYPRUS-2026

- **URL / accessed / type:** https://birdlifecyprus.org/cyprus-scops-owl/ ; 2026-11-11; current institution overview.
- **Facts:** 19–21 cm, 47–54 cm wingspan; hollows in conifers/olive trees and boxes; forests, farmland, villages and olive groves.
- **Limits/decision:** overview, not an ageing source; habitat/nesting context only.

### CYSO-IEZEKIEL-ETAL-2021
- **Title / authors / year:** “Nest-Box Occupancy by the Cyprus Scops Owl in Different Habitats” / Iezekiel et al. / 2021, *Animals* 11:1775.
- **DOI / URL / accessed:** https://doi.org/10.3390/ani11061775 ; 2026-11-11.
- **Type / scope:** primary 2015–2018 breeding study; 238 boxes in Paphos Forest rural, ecotone and forest sites; laying through fledging.
- **Facts:** boxes mainly on *Pinus brutia* or buildings; 5–11% occupancy; edge/rural occupancy higher.
- **Limits/decision:** no juvenile feather chronology or locomotor threshold; breeding-site context only.

### Reuse and corrected boundaries
- New1 / reused4 / corrected5. V3's pale warm-grey and tidy narrow pinstripes are corrected toward dark cool grey, broad irregular streaks, coarse vermiculation and larger isolated white spots. Cyprus wing data do not justify imposed female height. A photographed fledged stage does not establish exact age or sustained flight. Olive-grove context is documented but not universal. Science remains false.
- Links: [v4 research](species/111-otus-cyprius-v4.md); planned v4; run `production/runs/20261111T175057+0800-cycle-5.md`.

- **URL / accessed:** https://tanguydeville.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/2012-02-observations-at-a-nest-of-amazonian-pygmy-owl-glaucidium-hardyi-in-french-guiana-neotropical-birding-nc2b011.pdf ; accessed 2026-11-08.
- **Type / scope:** primary field observation and photographs at one nest.
- **Pages / figures actually read:** pp.23–26, especially nest description pp.23–24 and Figs.2–4.
- **Facts:** old woodpecker hole about 25 m high in a dead c.35 m tree, entrance c.7.5 cm; it contained almost full-grown young. Only one young was ever seen at the entrance. Adults entered directly rather than pausing on the rim. Fig.2 documents adult occipital false eyes.
- **Limits / confidence:** one nest and one visually observed young; no exact age, iris chronology, flight threshold or continuous feather series. High for cavity context and “almost full-grown” stage only.
- **Design use:** one almost-full-grown juvenile fully supported at the vertical cavity lip; no flight, leap or independence claim.


## 2026-11-08 — #33 *Taenioptynx brodiei* v5 — primary-paper re-read, current combination and 56-day fledgling boundary

### Re-read / correction — COOW-LIN-ETAL-2014
- **Title / authors / year:** “Colour Morphs in the Collared Pygmy Owl *Glaucidium brodiei* are Age-Related, not a Polymorphism” / Wen-Loung Lin, Si-Min Lin & Hui-Yun Tseng / 2014, *Ardea* 102(1):95–99.
- **DOI / URL / accessed:** https://doi.org/10.5253/078.102.0115 ; author-uploaded full text read at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/264422734_Colour_Morphs_in_the_Collared_Pygmy_Owl_Glaucidium_brodiei_are_Age-Related_not_a_Polymorphism ; accessed 2026-11-08.
- **Type / scope:** primary longitudinal nest-box, banding and recapture study at Lien-hua-chih, central Taiwan, supplemented by 68 museum specimens.
- **Facts actually read:** 63 owls were banded, including 32 nestlings. A known individual hatched 15 June 2010 and at first recapture on 10 August (56 days) was fully grown but retained fledgling plumage: fewer bars/spots on back and crown and an incompletely formed occipital pattern. At 165 days it was rufous with formed occipital pattern; at 394 and 720 days it was grey. The study concludes fledgling plumage occurs at 2–3 months, rufous at 4–7 months and definitive plumage at about 10–11 months. Adult/breeding-pair mass direction is male lighter than female, but measured ranges overlap (male 52–72 g; female 58–92 g).
- **Pages / figures:** printed pp.95–99; methods and mass p.96; results/discussion and Fig.3 pp.97–98.
- **Correction applied:** do not treat rufous and grey as stable sex-independent adult colour morphs. V5 uses definitive grey adults and a known-age 56-day fledgling with reduced dorsal/crown pattern and incomplete occipital marking. The overlapping masses permit only a subtle fuller female impression, not a universal height ratio.
- **Limits:** Taiwan study population; no quantitative wing/tail growth series or first-flight measurement. “Fully grown” does not establish independent flight performance. High confidence for the documented plumage sequence, moderate transfer outside the studied population.
- **Links:** research/species/33-taenioptynx-brodiei-v5.md; design/concepts/33-taenioptynx-brodiei-v5.png.

### Re-read / correction — COOW-ITIS-2026
- **Institution / records / accessed:** Integrated Taxonomic Information System; *Taenioptynx brodiei brodiei* TSN 1244720 and *Glaucidium brodiei brodiei* TSN 687017; accessed 2026-11-08.
- **URLs:** https://itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?print_version=PRT&search_topic=TSN&search_value=1244720&source=to_print ; https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?print_version=PRT&search_topic=TSN&search_value=687017&source=to_print
- **Facts actually read:** *Taenioptynx brodiei* is the valid species combination in the current hierarchy; *Glaucidium brodiei brodiei* is an invalid subsequent combination mapped to *Taenioptynx brodiei brodiei*. IOC World Bird List v15.1 is among the current record sources.
- **Limits / design use:** nomenclature only; does not support plumage, development or sex-size claims. Use current label *Taenioptynx brodiei* and preserve *Glaucidium brodiei* (and project historical *Noctua brodiei*) in the crosswalk.

## 2026-11-06 — #112 *Asio abyssinicus* v3 — nominate-adult identity and older-juvenile stage

### ABY-ITIS-555498-2026 — newly indexed current/old-name record
- Integrated Taxonomic Information System, TSN 555498, accessed 2026-11-06: https://itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?print_version=PRT&search_topic=TSN&search_value=555498&source=to_print
- Current valid *Asio abyssinicus*; original/invalid combination *Otus abyssinicus*. Two subspecies are listed: nominate *A. a. abyssinicus* and *A. a. graueri*. Taxonomy only; no morphology/development inference. High confidence for naming.

### ABY-COLLAR-BOESMAN-2019 — newly indexed primary museum/taxonomy study
- N. J. Collar & Peter Boesman, 2019, “The taxonomy of certain *Asio* and *Bubo* owl species in Africa and Arabia,” *Bulletin of the African Bird Club* 26(2):155–169: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/335292194_The_taxonomy_of_certain_Asio_and_Bubo_owl_species_in_Africa_and_Arabia
- Pages 158–161, Figs. 1–3, Tables 1–2 actually read. Compared with *A. otus*, *A. abyssinicus* has broader/fused dark upperpart markings, a denser net of underpart panels, curve-shaped pale spots rather than fine barring on secondaries/tail, and substantially larger bill/wing/tail means. Nominate birds tend more ochre-buff than smaller, greyer *graueri*. Sexes were pooled and only approximately balanced; this source does not support a fixed female-larger display. High confidence for specimen morphology; not a development source.

### ABY-MATON-1989-JUV — newly indexed species-labelled field photograph
- Peter Maton, “African Long-eared Owl (juv) (*Asio abyssinicus*),” photographed Ethiopia 1989; scanned slide uploaded 2011: https://www.flickr.com/photos/34579661@N04/5424426357
- Page and full browser image actually opened. Visible age-unknown older juvenile has charcoal/gray-brown loose down, a very dark face, orange irises, a dark bill with a narrow pale midface highlight, short emerging tufts, down-softened sides, concealed tail and branch/foliage support. The crop does not establish hatch age, sex, wing/tail chronology, foot anatomy or sustained flight. Medium confidence for visible stage and source label; not an ageing study.

### ABY-OGADA-MURIITHI-2017 — corrected/re-read field-project habitat limits
- Darcy Ogada & Paul Muriithi, 2017, African Bird Club final report, “Is the Abyssinian Owl on Mt Kenya dependent on declining heath forest habitat?”: https://www.africanbirdclub.org/sites/default/files/2016_Abyssinian_Owl.pdf
- Pages 1–5 actually read. The report documents extreme-highland distribution, a 1961 Kenya museum specimen from Hagenia woodland, preliminary suspected observations/roost evidence in heath and the authors’ explicit uncertainty about breeding/natural history. Design use is a generic montane-highland woodland/heath context only; suspected Mt Kenya roost/pellets cannot be turned into a confirmed nest or universal habitat. Medium-high for the project’s stated limits, low for species assignment of unconfirmed signs.

### ABY-ONET-LANNELUC-2018 — newly indexed dated adult photograph
- Catherine & Bernard Lanneluc, adult *A. abyssinicus*, Nov. 2018, Dinsho, Bale Mountains National Park, Ethiopia: https://www.oiseaux.net/photos/catherine.et.bernard.lanneluc/hibou.d.abyssinie.1.html
- Full field photograph and metadata opened. Supports nominate adult’s orange iris, black bill, tall but flexible central tufts, dark-rimmed warm facial disc, robust dark-gold streaked/barred body and feathered tarsi. One pose and lighting do not define universal colour, sex or tuft angle. Medium confidence for visible identity.

- Reused repository records: `ABO-COLLAR-BOESMAN-2019`, `ABO-OGADA-MURIITHI-2017` where present in v2 history; this update adds stable IDs without duplicating unsupported facts. User-uploaded Mikkola guide was not mounted in this execution, so no new page claim. Detailed boundaries and complete prompt: `research/species/112-asio-abyssinicus-v3.md`. Science remains false.

## 2026-11-06 — #100 *Strix huhula* v5 — directly described nestling/brancher boundary

### HUH-BC2013

- **Type / species / stage / facts:** primary nest monitoring of the Atlantic-forest subspecies under the historical combination *Ciccaba huhula albomarginata*. At the live angico tree fork, 15.2 m high and enclosed by vertical branches plus epiphytes, the 18 November nestling was mostly pale grey on body and wings with horizontal black barring, a black heart-shaped mask with white border, and yellow bill/legs; it walked actively. ## 2026-11-05 — #65 *Tyto soumagnei* v5 — no-visible-sex-dimorphism / down-only nestling boundary

### MRO-RAMAMONJISOA-2014-P56-57-75-77
- **Title / author / year:** *Étude de la biologie et de l’écologie d’Effraie de Soumagne Tyto soumagnei (Grandidier, 1878) dans la Nouvelle Aire Protégée de Bemanevika, Bealanana* — Juliot Carl Ramamonjisoa, Université d’Antananarivo doctoral thesis, defended 2014.
- **URL / pages / accessed:** https://protectedareas.mg/content/documents/ff1f419c-05a9-4910-88d5-22fde787ce37/f49d347156d2438f97d2c6b8df277bc1.pdf ; printed pp.56–57 and 75–77, plus Annex I; full PDF text and relevant passages read 2026-11-05.
- **Type / species / stages:** primary multi-year field thesis; eight sexed adults and three tree-hole nests, including down-covered nestlings of unknown exact age.
- **Facts:** the thesis explicitly states that no size, colour or form difference is visually detectable between male and female. In the measured sample, mean wingspan was nearly equal (male 771.5 ± 10.9 mm, female 769.5 ± 20.4 mm; n=4 each), while mean mass differed (male 298 ± 5.7 g, female 337.5 ± 10.4 g). Three nests were tree holes; entrances were 16–20 m high and internal depth 45–117 cm. In 2014, two chicks disappeared while still covered only in down and could not escape the cavity.
- **Limits / conflicts:** small adult sample; sexing used mass plus cloacal protuberance, not genetic sexing. The down-only chicks lack exact age, measurements, photographs in the extracted passage and feather chronology. Mass difference does not license a visible crown-height or silhouette ratio; inability to escape does not establish an exact locomotor threshold.
- **Design/check decision:** adults share equal display height and essentially the same silhouette/plumage; label sex without coding colour as sex. Depict one age-unknown down-covered nestling low on a deep cavity floor, with no long remiges, tail or branch/flight pose. The Bemanevika tree hole is a documented example, not universal habitat.
- **Links:** `research/species/65-tyto-soumagnei-v5.md`; planned concept v5; run `production/runs/20261105T153530+0800-cycle-1.md`.

## 2026-11-04 — #157 *Scotopelia bouvieri* v3 — riverine stick nest and down-rich young

### VFO-BROSSET-ERARD-1986-P63
- **Title / authors / year:** *Les oiseaux des régions forestières du Nord-Est du Gabon. I. Ecologie et comportement des espèces* — André Brosset & Christian Erard, 1986.
- **DOI / URL:** https://doi.org/10.3406/revec.1986.5179 ; https://www.persee.fr/doc/revec_1168-3651_1986_sup_41_3_5179?pageId=T1_63
- **Type / page / accessed:** primary long-term field account; species account navigated at Persée page view T1_63 (article pp.4–289); accessed 2026-11-04.
- **Facts read:** the species was associated with large rivers in NE Gabon; August nests were stick platforms in trees roughly 2.5–3 m above water, with only a few adult feathers; observed broods included one or two young around 40 days; another nest reused an old *Lampribis rara* nest; growth was unusually slow and one young estimated at 35 days still retained juvenile down about three months later.

## 2026-11-04 — #155 *Scotopelia ussheri* v3 — field-documented flying juvenile and adult separation

### RFO-MONTICELLI-KOROMA-BANNAH-2015-P183-188
- **Title / authors / year:** *Observations of Rufous Fishing Owl Scotopelia ussheri in Sierra Leone* — David Monticelli, Alusein P. Koroma & Denis Bannah, 2015.
- **URL:** https://www.researchgate.net/publication/281632427_Observations_of_Rufous_Fishing_Owl_Scotopelia_ussheri_in_Sierra_Leone
- **Type / accessed:** primary field observations with photographs; accessed 2026-11-04.
- **Scope / pages / figures:** adults and juvenile/immature; Bulletin of the African Bird Club 22(2), printed pp.183–188, especially pp.185–188 and Figs.1, 3–5.
- **Facts:** adult observed on raffia palm over a narrow slow river channel; upperparts are plain/mixed rufous, creamy-buff and white rather than uniformly finely barred; underparts finely dark-shaft streaked; bill bluish-grey with yellowish cere; unfeathered tarsi and toes yellowish-orange. The photographed juvenile was substantially smaller and stubbier, fluffier and slightly paler, had loose first-generation feathers, flew twice, and showed virtually adult-like uniformly dusky-barred rufous wings. Authors estimated 4–5 months if the assumed laying period is correct.
- **Limits / confidence:** high confidence for the photographed individual and behaviour; age is explicitly an inference, not a known hatch date; no sex-specific measurements and no nest description.
- **Design use:** center a smaller, stubby, pale-rufous, loose-feathered older juvenile with formed barred wings, natural two-foot branch grip and no helpless-chick pose; do not invent a nest. Adults remain near-equal because sex direction is unsupported.
- **Links:** `research/species/155-scotopelia-ussheri-v3.md`; concept v3; run `owl-pet/production/runs/20261104T220156+0800-cycle-6.md`.

- **Type / accessed:** photographic historical record; accessed 2026-11-04.
- **Scope / pages / figures:** one captive juvenile photographed 6 October 1993 and again six months later; Bulletin of the African Bird Club 29(1), printed pp.97–98, Figs.1–3.
- **Facts:** first photographs showed whitish downy plumage; the same individual had adult plumage six months later. The paper distinguishes this young downy stage from Monticelli et al.'s free-living pale-rufous juvenile.
- **Limits / confidence:** exact age at capture, locomotor capacity and intervening feather chronology are unknown; captive setting is not nest evidence.
- **Design use:** cross-check that pale/whitish juvenile stages exist, but use the better-behaviour-documented Monticelli older juvenile for v3 rather than inventing a downy nestling.

- **Title / institution / year:** *Scotopelia ussheri — Rufous Fishing-owl* — BirdLife International / IUCN Red List, assessed 2021.
- **URL / DOI:** https://doi.org/10.2305/IUCN.UK.2021-3.RLTS.T22689038A180213988.en

### ELWO-LIGON-1968-UMMZ-P34-35
- **Title / author / year:** *The Biology of the Elf Owl, Micrathene whitneyi* — J. David Ligon, 1968.
- **Institution / source type:** University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, Miscellaneous Publications No. 136; original monograph.

- **Facts read:** nestling period 28–33 d; at 17–18 d body contour feathers are present, upper wing coverts exceed the exposed remiges, feet are almost bare, head down remains; at 21–22 d first flight attempts occur, tail is about 1.7 cm and mostly sheathed, and longest primary is 3.8 cm with 2.1 cm still sheathed; 25–26 d birds still fly ineffectively and capable flight appears around 27–28 d.
- **Limits / confidence:** high for the reported Arizona sequence and measurements; not a color plate and not proof of identical timing in every individual/subspecies.
- **Design / review use:** juvenile at approximately 21–22 d, completely supported, with retained head down, mostly contoured body, nearly bare feet, upper coverts prominent, short partly sheathed remiges and an extremely short mostly sheathed tail. ## 2026-11-05 — #23 *Psiloscops flammeolus* v5 — one-week known-age feather boundary

### FLOW-RICHMOND-DEWEESE-PILLMORE-1980-P35-46
- **Title / authors / year:** *Brief Observations on the Breeding Biology of the Flammulated Owl in Colorado* — Merle L. Richmond, Lawrence R. DeWeese & Richard E. Pillmore, 1980.
- **URL / type / pages / accessed:** https://journal.westernfieldornithologists.org/index.php/westernbirds/article/download/305/297/582 ; primary field and captive-development paper, *Western Birds* 11:35–46; printed pp.35–46; accessed 2026-11-05.
- **Species / stages / facts:** historical name *Otus flammeolus*, current *Psiloscops flammeolus*. Printed p.37 reports reused cavities without obvious nest material except wood bits. Printed pp.40 and 44 describe/photograph young at about one and three weeks: at about one week dense down remains, white except for a few darkening primary feathers emerging as blood quills, with no evident tail; by three weeks the bird is generally gray, body juvenal-feathered, barred below, with developed wing/tail feathers but still-short tail. Printed p.44 also bounds behavior: around 25 d captive young could fly 0.5 m downward but not upward; directed flight was much later.
- **Limits / confidence:** direct species-specific evidence but sample was small, two photographed captive nestlings had uncertain exact ages and may have been developmentally retarded after starvation; do not turn “about one week” into an exact day or universal sequence. High confidence for the visible one-week boundary, moderate for timing generalization.
- **Design decision:** v5 selects the approximately one-week photographed stage: dense white down, only a few short dark primary blood quills, no tail, low fully supported in sparse cavity wood bits. No flight or standing inference.
- **Links:** `research/species/23-psiloscops-flammeolus-v5.md`; `production/runs/20261105T013100+0800-cycle-1.md`; planned `design/concepts/23-psiloscops-flammeolus-v5.png`.

## 2026-11-05 — #42 *Athene brama* v5 — 21–25-day plumage versus flight boundary

### SPOT-ALI-2015 — re-read primary developmental series
- **Title / authors / year:** *Nest trees, habitat and breeding biology of the spotted owlet Athene brama brama (Temminck, 1821) in human habitation and agricultural landscape of India* — Abdul Hameed Mohamed Samsoor Ali & Ramachandran Santhanakrishnan, 2015.
- **DOI / URL / type / pages / accessed:** https://doi.org/10.1080/21658005.2015.1061248 ; https://www.researchgate.net/publication/280385349_Nest_trees_habitat_and_breeding_biology_of_the_spotted_owletAthene_brama_bramaTemminck_1821_in_human_habitation_and_agricultural_landscape_of_India ; primary two-habitat field study, *Zoology and Ecology* 25(3):211–219, printed pp.214–216, re-read 2026-11-05.
- **Scope / facts:** 27 nests in Madurai district. Printed pp.215–216 and Figure 6 document 21–25 d young with white neck and eyebrow plumage, typical gray feathers appearing adult-like, and well-developed remiges/rectrices with white wing markings. Young looked fully adult-like at 26–30 d; fledging averaged 31.4 ± 2.67 d, range 28–33 d. Cavities were 3–15 m high; large banyan trees were commonly used.
- **Limits / correction:** adult-like feathers at 21–25 d do not establish flight or branch-leaving. V5 may show formed folded wings and early white markings, but keeps the bird cavity-supported and dependent.
- **Design use:** 21–25 d cavity-lip juvenile with shorter tail, soft rounded body and folded formed wing; no open-wing threat or flight.

### SPOT-PANDE-2011 — re-read growth and sex boundary
- **Title / authors / year:** *Biometry based ageing of nestling Indian Spotted Owlets (Athene brama brama)* — Pande et al., 2011.
- **DOI / URL / type / pages / accessed:** https://doi.org/10.3897/zookeys.132.1346 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3208435/ ; primary known-age growth study, *ZooKeys* 132:75–88, methods and results, re-read 2026-11-05.
- **Scope / facts:** 53 active nests; eight known-age nestlings measured from hatching through fledging, 0–32 d, with 136 measurements. Sexes were externally alike and nestlings could not be separated by sex. The paper estimates acquisition of flight from biometry rather than external resemblance.
- **Limits / correction:** small intensive longitudinal sample and southern Indian subspecies. It supports equal external sex treatment and separating plumage maturity from locomotor ability, not a universal standing-height ratio.
- **Design use:** adults near equal; juvenile locomotion remains conservatively bounded.

### UROW-KAZAMA-JBBA-2005-P28-32
- **Title / author / year:** *Notes on Breeding Ecology of Ural Owl in Niigata Prefecture* — Kazama, 2005.

- **Scope / facts:** fifty nest boxes were monitored, twenty were used, and 43 chicks were banded. For roughly the first two weeks after exiting the nest, fledglings remained on branches within about 30 m and were provisioned by adults.
- **Limits / design use:** the paper supports natural branch support and continued dependence after nest exit, not exact day-29 plumage, first-flight strength, or a universal distance. The juvenile remains supported and dependent; no independent flight or hunting pose.

### UROW-ERIKSSON-1984-P313-316 — re-read primary growth series
- **Title / authors / year:** *Growth and survival of Ural Owl nestlings* — Eriksson, Lundberg & Westman, 1984.
- **URL / type / pages / accessed:** https://www.annzool.net/PDF/anzf21/anz21-313-316.pdf ; primary multi-nest growth study, *Annales Zoologici Fennici* 21:313–316; re-read 2026-11-05.
- **Facts:** eyes open around day 3 and feathers emerge around day 5. Wing length and fourth-primary sheath length predict age with about one-day mean error. Adult females are clearly larger, but size dimorphism is not visible until the end of the nestling period.
- **Limits / correction:** the printed graph was not used to invent an exact day-29 wing length. Adult female size is shown moderately; the unsexed juvenile is not sex-scaled.

- **Scope / facts:** five captive pairs and 27 young; the mesoptile begins around day 5 and covers the body by about day 16; wing quill sheaths appear around day 10, while the tail begins much later (around day 28).
- **Limits / use:** captive chronology is a species-specific boundary but not a universal wild schedule. V5 shows a mesoptile-dominant day-29 bird with a short folded wing and little/hidden tail, not adult remiges.

## 2026-11-05 — #45 *Strix seloputo* v5 — dated brancher, balance-flap and first-flight boundary

### SOWL-BESG-2022-P1 — re-read dated family record
- **Title / author / year:** *Spotted wood owl (Strix seloputo) family at Pasir Ris Park, Singapore: Part 1* — LW Teo / Bird Ecology Study Group, 2022.
- **URL / type / sections / accessed:** https://besgroup.org/2022/02/27/spotted-wood-owl-strix-seloputo-family-at-pasir-ris-park-singapore-part-1/ ; dated field-photography chronology, paragraphs 19–27 and photo captions; re-read 2026-11-05.
- **Facts:** one pair nested in a bird's-nest fern about 5 m up a rain tree. Part 1 dates the first fledging to 18 February and the second to 21 February 2022. The owlets moved precariously along branches and flapped while walking to maintain balance; parents watched from nearby branches.
- **Limits / design use:** one family and one site. The fern/rain-tree setting is contextual, not universal nest architecture. Balance flapping is not independent flight.

### SOWL-BESG-2022-P2 — re-read growth and locomotion chronology
- **Title / author / year:** *Spotted wood owl (Strix seloputo) family at Pasir Ris Park, Singapore: Part 2* — LW Teo / Bird Ecology Study Group, 2022.
- **URL / type / sections / accessed:** https://besgroup.org/2022/04/01/spotted-wood-owl-strix-seloputo-family-at-pasir-ris-park-singapore-part-2/ ; dated follow-up field chronology, paragraphs 18–24 and captions/video notes; re-read 2026-11-05.
- **Facts:** on fledging the owlets were about half adult size; remiges lengthened over weeks while rectrices remained shorter. A 23 February video shows branch walking with wing flaps for balance. By 11 March they were observed flying branch-to-branch; by 24 March their patterns were adult-like while down remained visible on the head.
- **Conflict / correction:** Part 2 dates the first fledging to 19 February, one day later than Part 1. The design therefore uses the conservative label “2–4 days post-fledging in one documented family” for the 23 February observation and does not assert an exact hatch age.

- **Title / author / year:** *An owlet fell from its nest…* — YC Wee / Bird Ecology Study Group, 2018.
- **URL / type / sections / accessed:** https://besgroup.org/2018/05/04/an-owlet-fell-from-its-nest/ ; dated field observation and rescue note, paragraphs 27–42; accessed 2026-11-05.
- **Facts:** an age-unknown *S. seloputo* chick walked, flapped and scrambled up a trunk but was unable to fly; after losing grip it fell, and was moved to a stable raised surface.
- **Limits / design use:** no age or feather chronology. It supports the requirement for visible support and the inference boundary that flapping/scrambling does not prove flight.

- **Facts:** current name *Strix seloputo* Horsfield, 1821; earless head, bold black-barred buffy underparts, dark brown upperparts with white spots, dark brown eyes, grey bill and feathered tarsi; forest/woodland.
- **Limits:** adult account; no sex-size direction or juvenile developmental sequence.

Typical photographed setting is a top-opening natural cavity in an old mango tree in farmland; other large trees/groves occur.

- **Scope / facts:** repository-indexed field serial measurements support a day-34–36 nest-leaving bird moving from an open-top cavity to an adjacent branch by walking; tarsus and beak were about 90% of adult measures while wing and tail were about 50%.

## 2026-11-05 — #59 *Ketupa zeylonensis* v5 — Hong Kong brancher and full-resolution boundary

### BFOW-HKBWS-AVIFAUNA-2026
- **Title / institution / accessed:** Brown Fish Owl species account — *The Avifauna of Hong Kong*, Hong Kong Bird Watching Society; accessed 2026-11-05.

- **Species/stage/facts:** *Ketupa zeylonensis* adults and Hong Kong young. Adults 48–55 cm with loose ear tufts, usually yellow eyes, grey bill, long unfeathered legs/pale-yellow feet, white throat and heavily streaked/crossbarred plumage. Some juveniles are paler on mantle/coverts/scapulars, with narrower/sparser breast streaks and smaller tufts. Seven nest sites included roofs, ledges, buttress roots and a natural hollow; date ranges distinguish downy chicks, unfledged juveniles, first flight and post-fledging dependency.
- **Limits/conflicts/credibility:** institutional synthesis from regional records, not a known-age feather series; dates overlap, light angle alters apparent iris colour and no sexed measurements are supplied. High value for Hong Kong identity/habitat/stage boundaries; not an exact-age or universal-nest source.
- **Design/check decision:** bare tarsi, local waterside woodland, paler smaller-tuft juvenile and nest-form diversity; no exact age, universal nest or adult size multiplier.

### BFO-INDIANBIRDS-2013-P147-151
- **Title / authors / year:** “Notes on the breeding of the Brown Fish Owl *Ketupa zeylonensis*” — Raju Vyas, Kartik Upadhayay, Mital R. Patel, Rahul D. Bhatt & Pritesh Patel, 2013.

- **Facts:** active fluffy-faced 15–20-day chicks had smaller body/wing feathers; ear tufts developed later. Near departure the two young were almost adult-sized, stayed 4–6 days in the same tree canopy and remained parent-dependent. Paired adults could sometimes be separated by size when together.

- **Title / authors / year:** “Observations on the Breeding of the Brown Fish-Owl *Ketupa zeylonensis* in Kerala, Southern India” — T. N. Bindu & Peroth Balakrishnan, 2015.
- **DOI / URL / type / pages:** https://doi.org/10.17087/jbnhs/2015/v112i2/104938 ; primary nine-year field note, *JBNHS* 112(2):97–98; full text re-read 2026-11-05.

## 2026-11-05 — #70 *Ninox strenua* v5 — photographic sex boundary and first-flight restraint

### POWERFUL-COOKE-ETAL-2020
- **Title / authors / year:** “Photography can determine the sex of a predator with limited sexual dimorphism: A case study of the powerful owl” — Cooke, Rendall, Weston, Porch, Bradsworth & White, 2020.
- **DOI / URL:** https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gecco.2020.e00959 ; https://www.researchgate.net/publication/339096218_Photography_can_determine_the_sex_of_a_predator_with_limited_sexual_dimorphism_A_case_study_of_the_powerful_owl
- **Type / pages / accessed:** open-access peer-reviewed primary photographic-morphometric study, *Global Ecology and Conservation* 22:e00959, pp.1–8, especially pp.2–6 and Figs.1–6; full article text read 2026-11-05.
- **Species/stage/facts:** adult *Ninox strenua*. Sixty-three known-sex front-facing alert photographs supplied the measured model; the head-width/inter-nostril ratio was larger in males. In 82 assessable images, female facemask feathers reached or slightly exceeded the horizontal head contour whereas male facemask feathers stopped short. Overall sexual dimorphism was described as extremely limited.
- **Limits/conflicts/credibility:** the method requires direct forward alert posture and image ratios; posture, angle and feather fluff distort measurement, and the male mask-to-contour gap can be small. Strong primary evidence for a restrained front-view diagnostic, not a fixed stylised pixel ratio or conspicuous height difference.
- **Design/check decision:** keep adult crown/support height comparable; use only a subtly broader male head/body and a female mask edge reaching the head contour. Do not exaggerate scale or invent dichromatism.
- **Links:** `research/species/70-ninox-strenua-v5.md`; planned concept v5; run `production/runs/20261105T173620+0800-cycle-6.md`.

## 2026-11-06 — #82 *Otus senegalensis* v5 — documented day-22 nest-box stage

### SEN-RIEKERT-1986-P425-428

- **Title / author / year:** “Some observations on the breeding biology of the African Scops Owl” — B. R. Riekert, 1986, *Madoqua* 14(4):425–428.
- **URL / pages / accessed:** https://the-eis.com/elibrary/sites/default/files/downloads/literature/Riekert_1986_Madoqua_14_4_African_Scops_Owl.pdf ; complete four-page PDF and page images read 2026-11-06; printed pp.425–428, especially pp.425–426.
- **Type / species / stage:** primary nest-box field study near Windhoek; one measured adult pair and several broods, with daily development notes.
- **Facts:** the measured pair had equal 140 mm wing chords while the female weighed 110 g and male 70 g; plumage was described as almost identical (p.425). Wing feathers emerged from sheaths at about day 14; by day 22 body feathers, including the tail, had largely emerged, and young called and scratched at the nest-box entrance; one brood left at day 23 (p.426). Nest boxes were used because cavities were limited in the arid woodland.
- **Limits / conflicts:** one adult pair cannot establish a universal mass or visible-size ratio. The study text does not provide a continuous photographic feather atlas, individual sex, or sustained-flight threshold. A later two-pair study reported a 25–28-day nestling period, so departure age varies and is not transferred to every bird.
- **Design decision:** depict a clearly labelled day-22 **study stage** on a broad nest-box sill, both feet supported, calling/scratching at the entrance; residual down plus largely emerged body/tail feathers, compact non-adult wing and no flight. Keep adult wing length/height equal; female may be subtly fuller in body mass but not taller.
- **Links:** `research/species/82-otus-senegalensis-v5.md`; planned v5 concept/review; run `production/runs/20261106T034111+0800-cycle-6.md`.

### SEN-ITIS-1063416-2026

- **Facts/use:** *Scops senegalensis* Swainson, 1837 is the invalid original combination; valid name is *Otus senegalensis* (Swainson, 1837). Taxonomy only; no morphology or development inference.

- **Title / authors / year:** “A new species of scops-owl … from Príncipe Island and novel insights into the systematic affinities within *Otus*” — Melo et al., 2022, *ZooKeys* 1126:1–54.

- **Facts:** the article treats mainland African *O. senegalensis* as part of the African subclade and lists 15 geographically broad museum specimens with wing lengths about 103–145 mm and tail lengths 40–65 mm.

## 2026-11-07 — #138 *Otus mentawi* v4 — complete-image recovery and juvenile-stage recheck

### MEN-TAUFIQURRAHMAN-2018-P31-32 — newly indexed primary field-development record
- **Title / authors / year:** “First breeding record of Mentawai Scops Owl *Otus mentawi*, with notes on the morphology and vocalisations of juveniles”, Imam Taufiqurrahman, Ismael Saumanuk & Arif Setiawan, 2018.
- **URL / access:** https://swaraowa.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/05/mentawai-scops-owl.pdf ; accessed 2026-11-07.
- **Type / pages / scope:** primary field observation; BirdingASIA 29, printed pp.31–32; west Siberut adults and two dated, branch-using juveniles observed 12–21 May 2017.
- **Useful source facts:** the adult usually called high while a juvenile called from a lower branch, sometimes 2–3 m above ground; by 18 May two juveniles were slightly smaller than the adult. They had pale greyish-brown underparts with thin dark streaks, darker upperparts, reddish-brown faces and eyes, pale greyish-horn bills/toes, short dark tails, and folded wings projecting beyond the tail with faint narrow bars that strengthened by 21 May.
- **Limits / confidence:** exact hatch dates were not known; the paper’s roughly 25-day incubation/fledging chronology is explicitly comparative and only a reasonable estimate. It does not document sex-specific standing-size ratio or continuous flight ability. High confidence for the photographed dated plumage/support stage.
- **Design decision:** use the later documented juvenile stage on a natural lower branch with both feet supported; retain formed but non-adult wings beyond a short tail, and do not label exact age or flight competence.
- **Links:** `research/species/138-otus-mentawi-v4.md`; target `design/concepts/138-otus-mentawi-v4.png`.

- **Type / pages / scope:** photographic species account; PDF pages 168–169 / printed pp.166–167; adult *Otus mentawi*.
- **Useful source facts:** length about 20 cm, wing 157–166 mm; no data on sexual size differences; rufous adults have dark reddish-brown upperparts, no nuchal collar, a whitish-and-black scapular row, mottled dark-brown wing coverts, reddish-brown/chestnut underparts with herringbone marks and white ocelli, brown (sometimes yellow) eyes, yellowish-horn bill, fully feathered tarsi and bare flesh-coloured toes with powerful dark claws. Lowland rainforest plus secondary growth/villages are within habitat.
- **Limits / confidence:** the guide said juvenile unknown before the 2018 field paper; one photographic account cannot define every individual palette. High confidence for adult identity and the absence of quantified sex-size direction.

## 2026-11-07 — #139 *Otus jolandae* v4 source delta

### RIN-SANGSTER-2013-P8-11 — verified primary description
- **Title / authors / year:** “A New Owl Species of the Genus *Otus* (Aves: Strigidae) from Lombok, Indonesia”, George Sangster, Ben F. King, Philippe Verbelen & Colin R. Trainor, 2013.
- **URL / DOI:** https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0053712 ; open full text: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0053712
- **Access / type / pages:** read 2026-11-07; peer-reviewed open primary species description, pp.8–11 and diagnosis/holotype sections; species and one specimen retaining juvenile feathers.
- **Useful source facts:** current species was separated from the Lombok population long treated as *O. magicus albiventris*; adults are dark cinnamon-brown and less boldly patterned, with warm cinnamon breast and paler finely barred belly; holotype label records golden-yellow iris, brown bill and dull-ochre feet. Female AMNH 629942 retained scattered white to buffy-white juvenile feathers with brown spots/bars on crown and nape. The paper documents degraded/secondary forest and elevations 25–1350 m.
- **Limits / confidence:** seven historical specimens and field adult photographs; the retained juvenile feathers occur on one female specimen and do not define a complete juvenile stage, exact age, iris chronology, flight ability or population sex-size relation. High confidence for diagnosis and historical-name context; limited for development.
- **Design decision:** render an age-unknown older immature, not a chick: smaller/fluffier, formed but softened wing and short tail, with only scattered pale retained crown/nape feathers. Keep adults comparable in displayed scale and avoid repeated bright covert spots.
- **Links:** `research/species/139-otus-jolandae-v4.md`; target `design/concepts/139-otus-jolandae-v4.png`.

- **Useful source facts:** about 23 cm, 115 g, wing 148–157 mm; no sexual-size data; relatively long ear tufts, warm-brown upperparts, whitish scapular band, golden-yellow eyes, blackish-brown bill, rusty underparts with irregular pale/rich-brown marks, legs feathered to dull-ochre toe bases; forested and degraded habitats to 1350 m.

## 2026-11-12 — #142 *Asio grammicus* v4 research delta

### JAM-GOSSE-1847-P19-23 — original description and immature observations
- **Title / author / year:** *The Birds of Jamaica* / Philip Henry Gosse / 1847.
- **Stable ID / original access:** Biodiversity Heritage Library title 14540, DOI https://doi.org/10.5962/bhl.title.14540 ; Project Gutenberg full transcription https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/73391/pg73391-images.html ; accessed and read 2026-11-12.
- **Locator/type:** printed pp.19–23; original species description and field/captive observations; historical primary source.
- **Species/stage:** original *Ephialtes grammicus*; current *Asio grammicus*; adult male/female and two immature females.
- **Facts:** printed p.19 supports hazel irides, pale blue-grey bill, dull lead feet, blackish-grey cere, dusky-brown/umber plumage, c.1-inch conical ear tufts, black-edged pale-umber face, fine blackish pencilling, bright-umber breast with wavy mottling/dark shaft dashes, plainer fawn belly/thighs/vent and a fully feathered tarsus. Gosse's female agreed with Robinson's adult male except warm-colour terminology. Printed pp.20–22 record two downy immature females: one flew to a nearby tree after disturbance; another fell from a shaken small tree and lay helpless by day.
- **Limits/conflict/confidence:** nineteenth-century colour vocabulary and individual anecdotes; the two immatures have no exact age, sex comparison, feather-sequence or standardized flight test. High confidence for the explicitly described visible adult characters and existence of downy immature variation; low for generalizing locomotor ability.
- **Design/check support:** adults near-equal/same palette; blue-grey bill, dull lead feet, feathered tarsi; an older down-remnant juvenile must not automatically be rendered wingless, but no flight is depicted. Links `research/species/142-asio-grammicus-v4.md` and v4 prompt/review.

- **Title / author / year:** *Illustrations of the Birds of Jamaica* / Philip Henry Gosse / 1849.
- **URL / locator / type:** https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/49061937 ; Plate IV, “Ephialtes grammicus,” reference to printed p.19; accessed 2026-11-12; historical primary illustration.
- **Species/stage:** original *Ephialtes grammicus*; adult illustration.
- **Value/use:** corroborates the compact eared-owl silhouette, warm umber palette and dark facial framing used in the original account.
- **Limits:** a single period plate, not a calibrated colour photograph and not juvenile or sex-dimorphism evidence. Used only as an adult silhouette/palette cross-check.

### JAM-PEREGRINE-FUND-2026 — habitat and explicit development unknowns
- **Institution/title/date:** The Peregrine Fund, Global Raptor Information Network species account “Jamaican Owl”; page accessed 2026-11-12; institutional synthesis, publication date not shown.
- **URL/sections:** https://peregrinefund.org/explore-raptors-species/owls/jamaican-owl ; “Where they live,” “Nesting” and species-description sections read.
- **Species/stage:** *Asio grammicus*; adult habitat and generalized breeding summary.
- **Facts:** associated mainly with lowland open woodland, forest edge, gardens/parks and agricultural areas; nest site summarized as tree cavity or tree fork; the account explicitly states that nestling growth, first-flight age and parental-care details remain unknown.
- **Limits/use:** secondary institutional synthesis without primary-page locators; it does not support a particular juvenile posture or nest construction. Used to select a leafy Jamaican edge habitat and to preserve development unknowns; no nest is depicted.

## 2026-11-07 — #161 *Ketupa blakistoni* v3 — Hokkaido scope, late-nestling stage and 2026 split

### BLF-BIRDRESEARCH-HAYASHI-2010-P1-4 — newly re-read institutional ecological guide
- **Title / author / institution / year:** “Blakiston’s Fish Owl”; Yoshihiro Hayashi / Japan Bird Research Association, *Bird Research News* 7(2), 2010.
- **URL:** https://www.bird-research.jp/1_shiryo/seitai/shimafukuro.pdf
- **Accessed / type:** 2026-11-07; institutional species guide citing field work and literature; full indexed text actually read. Screenshot rendering of PDF pp.3–4 failed after text retrieval and is recorded as a tooling limit.
- **Pages / stage:** printed pp.1–4; p.3 breeding and nesting; p.4 growth/dispersal; Photo 2 caption identifies a nestling at about 50 days.
- **Facts:** riparian broadleaf/mixed forest beside rivers, lakes, marshes and seashore; ice-free water is important. Female broods while male provisions. Natural nests are chiefly cavities in very large broadleaf trees; nest boxes are also used, with rare kite-nest/cliff-ledge cases. Incubation 35–38 days; usual fledging 48–60 days, one 69-day report; young are normally fed until autumn and sometimes winter.
- **Design/check use:** choose the directly documented ~50-day late nestling, low and fully supported at a large-tree cavity threshold; do not claim flight. Use Hokkaido riverine old-growth rather than a generic nest bowl.
- **Limits/confidence:** high for quoted guide facts and the pictured/captioned stage; synthesis rather than a single controlled development series. It does not provide a feather-tract timetable or individual flight test.

### BLF-HAYASHI-1997-283-285 — newly indexed primary telemetry note
- **Title / author / year:** “Home Range, Habitat Use and Natal Dispersal of Blakiston’s Fish-Owls”; Yoshihiro Hayashi, 1997, *Journal of Raptor Research* 31(3):283–285.
- **URL:** https://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/jrr/v031n03/p00283-p00285.pdf
- **Accessed / type:** 2026-11-07; primary field/radio-telemetry paper; pp.283–285 actually read.
- **Facts:** Hokkaido population depends on riparian forest; fledglings had been colour-marked since 1987; one radio-tagged male fledgling remained in its natal area for about a year before dispersal.
- **Design/check use:** supports an extended post-fledging dependence context and strict riparian setting, but not plumage reconstruction.
- **Limits/confidence:** high for tracked individuals; no exact plumage, sex-dimorphism or 50-day locomotor description.

### BLF-CLEMENTS-2026-SPLIT — newly indexed current taxonomy change
- **Title / institution / date:** “2026 Taxonomy Update”; Clements/eBird taxonomy, Cornell Lab of Ornithology, October 2026.
- **URL:** https://www.birds.cornell.edu/clementschecklist/updates-corrections-october-2026/
- **Accessed / type:** 2026-11-07; current institutional checklist update, section “Northern Fish-Owl”.
- **Facts:** Northern Fish-Owl *Ketupa doerriesi* is split from Blakiston’s Fish-Owl *K. blakistoni*. The retained *K. blakistoni* is monotypic and restricted to Hokkaido/northern Japan and adjacent insular Russia; continental northeast Asian birds are *K. doerriesi*. The update cites vocal and plumage differences including a white nape patch and tail pattern.
- **Design/check use:** v3 is explicitly Hokkaido *K. blakistoni* sensu stricto and must not borrow the conspicuous white nape/back patch or near-white tail of continental *doerriesi*. Historical broad-sense *Bubo/Ketupa blakistoni* references are scope-checked before transfer.
- **Limits/confidence:** high for current Clements/eBird treatment; other authorities may update on different schedules. This naming correction does not itself establish development.

### Reuse and evidence boundary
- Reused repository records **BLF-MIKKOLA-2013-P296**, **BLF-OWLPAGES-2020**, **BLF-MOVIN-2022** and **BLF-IOC13-1-2023** only within their previously indexed limits. The user-uploaded Mikkola guide was not mounted in this execution, so no fresh page claim is made.
- Adult plumage is alike; measured mass direction supports a fuller/heavier female but not a fixed standing-height ratio. Exact 50-day flight ability, continuous feather chronology, individual feather map and universal sex ratio remain unknown.
- Full prompt: [PROMPTS_FULL.md](../production/PROMPTS_FULL.md#161-ketupa-blakistoni-v3-2026-11-07). Research card: [161 v3](species/161-ketupa-blakistoni-v3.md). Scientific verification remains false.

## 2026-11-11 — #118 *Megascops cooperi* v5 — museum/live-character key, original description and current taxonomy

### PSC-CAMACHO-VARELA-2014-MEGASCOPS
- Camacho-Varela, Pablo. “¿Cómo identificar correctamente los búhos *Megascops* presentes en Costa Rica?” *Zeledonia* 18(2), 2014, pp.3–14. Asociación Ornitológica de Costa Rica.
- URL: https://www.avesdecostarica.org/uploads/7/0/1/0/70104897/18-2-completo.pdf ; accessed 2026-11-11.
- Actually read: printed p.4 key; pp.5–7 Figs.2–3 and explanatory text; pp.8–10 Figs.4 and 6 plus comparison discussion.
- Species-specific adult facts: fully feathered tarsi, bristled/hairy toes, pale gray-whitish ground colour, less-distinct dark facial rim, whitish-green bill/cere, no rufous phase reported for Costa Rica. Museum specimen and live-bird images independently show the tarsus/toe boundary. Ear tufts occur in all four compared species and may be hidden, so tufts alone are not diagnostic.
- Design support: adult leg/foot treatment, green-white bill/cere, pale non-rufous palette and restrained tuft use.
- Limits/conflicts: adult-only identification paper; it does not establish juvenile chronology, flight ability or a reliable sex-size display rule. PDF screenshot endpoint failed during this execution, but the full text and figure captions were actually read.
- Confidence: high for the stated Costa Rican adult diagnostic characters; not a juvenile source.

### PSC-RIDGWAY-1878-COOPERI
- Ridgway, Robert. “A Review of the American Species of the Genus *Scops*.” *Proceedings of the United States National Museum* 1 (1878), species account p.116.
- Smithsonian PDF: https://repository.si.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/0a67e5bb-28e6-447b-8441-f150bbed1c5f/content ; accessed 2026-11-11.
- Actually read: printed p.116, original adult female description from Santa Ana, Costa Rica. It records distinctly bristled toes, grayish umber-brown upperparts, fine dusky vermiculation, chain-like blackish mesial streaks, white-spotted scapular webs, pale-fulvous primary spots, face finely barred, yellow iris and yellowish-green cere/bill/feet.
- Design support: historical diagnostic texture and toe bristles; helps avoid generic polka dots.
- Limits: one historical adult female specimen description, archaic taxonomy and no juvenile development evidence.
- Confidence: high for the specimen description; limited generality.

### PSC-ITIS-686661-2026
- Integrated Taxonomic Information System, TSN 686661, *Megascops cooperi*; accessed 2026-11-11.
- URL: https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?print_version=PRT&search_topic=TSN&search_value=686661&source=to_print
- Current accepted species name: *Megascops cooperi* (Ridgway, 1878). Historical synonyms retained: *Otus cooperi* and *Scops cooperi*. Two direct subspecies are listed, *M. c. cooperi* and *M. c. lambi*.
- Design support: current title and old-name mapping only.
- Limits: taxonomy database, not morphology or development evidence.

The 18–21 May 2017 juveniles were slightly smaller than the adult, lower-branch users with pale greyish-brown thin-streaked underparts, darker upperparts, reddish-brown face/eyes, pale greyish-horn bill/toes, wing beyond a short dark tail and faint narrow flight-feather bars. - **MEN-ITIS-555383-2026:** current valid *Otus mentawi* and synonym/protonym *O. bakkamoena mentawi* re-read from the current ITIS/IOC-backed record. Taxonomy only.
- **MEN-MIKKOLA-2013-P166-167:** repository-stable prior actual read reused for adult identity and the explicit absence of sexual-size data. Uploaded guide unavailable in this execution; no fresh page claim.
- **MEN-CHASEN-KLOSS-1926-DOI:** publisher metadata and p.279 citation/protonym opened; full species text not read, so retained as an unverified morphology lead.

## 2026-11-12 — #139 *Otus jolandae* v5 — retained-juvenile-feather correction

### JOL-SANGSTER-ETAL-2013
- **Title/authors/year/type:** “A New Owl Species of the Genus *Otus* (Aves: Strigidae) from Lombok, Indonesia” / Sangster, King, Verbelen & Trainor / 2013 / peer-reviewed primary original description.

- **Pages/sections:** article pp.1–13; online lines 155–173, 280–354, 374–388; Fig.1 and Fig.S1.
- **Facts:** adults are dark cinnamon brown above, with warm cinnamon breast contrasting with whitish finely barred belly; golden-yellow iris, dark/brown bill, dull-ochre feet, tarsal feathering to toe bases. One female had paler breast, narrower head streaking and larger pale median-covert spots. Female AMNH 629942 retained scattered white/buffy juvenile crown/nape feathers but was not described as an all-over downy chick. Habitat includes solid, degraded and secondary forest/tree patches from 25–1350 m.
- **Limits/design:** type series is only seven specimens; individual female differences are not a universal sex-size rule. Exact immature age, iris, feather chronology, flight and nest are unknown. V5 uses a near-adult supported immature with only scattered retained juvenile head feathers.

## 2026-11-12 — #141 *Otus magicus* v5 — museum-series juvenile-wing and tarsal-boundary correction

### MAG-FINSCH-1898-P163-172 — newly indexed primary museum series
- **Title / author / year:** “Über *Scops magicus* (S. Müll.) und die verwandten Arten” / Otto Finsch / 1898, *Notes from the Leyden Museum* 20:163–180, plates 9–10.
- **URL / accessed / type:** https://repository.naturalis.nl/pub/508788/NLM1898020002009.pdf ; accessed 2026-11-12; primary comparative museum study.
- **Pages actually read:** printed pp.163–172, especially pp.163–164 and 170–172.
- **Species/stages:** 94-specimen *Scops magicus* complex; Batjan/Halmahera `leucospilus`, younger male and downy/nest-plumage young.
- **Facts:** colour/pattern vary widely and age/sex dependence was not established. Downy young with remiges/rectrices at differing development show fine dark crossbars; remiges may be as distinctly barred as adults. Tarsi are usually feathered near the toe bases but some specimens, including nest-plumage birds, have only the upper approximately two-thirds feathered and the rear surface bare. Tail barring varies too much for a universal exact count.
- **Limits/conflicts/credibility:** historical prepared series and broad old complex, not a known-age live growth sequence. High for the described specimens; no exact age, iris, flight, dependence, modern population ratio or nest inference.
- **Design/review decision:** allow a short partly down-veiled developing barred wing without turning the young into a miniature adult; show near-toe tarsal feathering with small irregular exposure, not a precise metric band; avoid exact repeated adult pattern counts.
- **Links:** `research/species/141-otus-magicus-v5.md`; planned v5 concept/review/run.

### Reused/re-read stable evidence
- `MAG-SHARPE-1875-P70-PLVI`: pp.70–74 and Plate VI reopened for historical adult-female `leucospilus` pattern and greyish-white cheek/ear-coverts; not treated as a dated development series.
- `MAG-ITIS-555379-2026`: current valid *Otus magicus*, original/synonym *Strix magica*, and valid *O. m. leucospilus* crosswalk reopened; taxonomy only.
- `MAG-MIKKOLA-2013-P189-190`: repository-pinned prior read reused; uploaded guide unavailable this execution, so no fresh page claim.
- **Index delta:** new verified 1; reused/re-read 3; corrected boundaries 3 (juvenile wing pattern, tarsal-feather variability, non-universal adult pattern counts). Detailed source facts, design boundary and complete prompt: `research/species/141-otus-magicus-v5.md`. Scientific verification remains false.

Tarsus values are 1.30, 1.40 and 1.40 in; middle toe s.u. 0.90, 1.10 and 1.10 in. The OCR damages sex symbols and renders “7.60” as “7-GO”, so the table was interpreted against the preceding statement “two males and a female” and the three-row order.

- Reread facts and design limits are recorded in `research/species/155-scotopelia-ussheri-v4.md`: older juvenile smaller/stubbier/paler/loose-feathered and observed flying with dusky-barred rufous wings (Monticelli et al. 2015 pp.185–188, Figs.1,3–5); whitish-down captive juvenile and adult plumage six months later without exact early age or action capacity (Koppetsch & Böhme 2022 pp.97–98, Figs.1–3); orange dark-eyed untufted adult and riverine habitat (IUCN 2021 Identification; Habitat & Ecology).
- Current/old-name mapping retained: *Scotopelia ussheri* Sharpe, 1871; historical combination *Bubo ussheri*.
- Still unknown: exact age and hatch date, sex-size direction, continuous feather sequence, first-flight threshold, nest site/material and universality of one juvenile's pattern.
- Links: `research/species/155-scotopelia-ussheri-v4.md`; run `owl-pet/production/runs/20261112T181053+0800-cycle-6.md`; planned concept `design/concepts/155-scotopelia-ussheri-v4.png`.


## 2026-11-12 — #156 *Scotopelia peli* v4 — three-month juvenile calibration

### PEL-MIKKOLA-2013-P304-306
- **Source:** Heimo Mikkola, *Owls of the World: A Photographic Guide*, 2nd ed., 2013; uploaded user PDF pp.306–308 / printed pp.304–306; read 2026-11-12.
- **Taxon/stages:** historical *Bubo peli* = current *Scotopelia peli*; adult, downy chick, mesoptile and first full plumage.
- **Facts:** 51–63 cm, 2055–2325 g; sexes alike in colour, female larger/sometimes paler; no real ear-tufts; blackish-brown eyes; bare straw legs/toes with fishing spicules; white chick; whitish/dull-yellow mesoptile with paler adult-like wing/tail; first full plumage paler and adult-like by about ten months.
- **Limit/decision:** photographic guide rather than known-age growth series. Supports adult identity and a partly formed, powder-down-softened older juvenile; does not set an exact wild flight threshold or fixed sex display ratio.

### PEL-PRAGUE-ZOO-2024-3MO
- **Source:** Prague Zoo, “The First Zoo in the World! Pel’s Fishing Owl Bred at Prague Zoo,” 29 Apr 2024, lines 44–60; https://www.zoopraha.cz/en/about-zoo/news/14677-the-first-zoo-in-the-world-pel-s-fishing-owl-bred-at-prague-zoo ; read 2026-11-12.
- **Stage/facts:** known three-month captive juvenile, light-coloured with remnants of powder down, photographed sitting beside parents after return to an improvised cavity.
- **Limit/decision:** captive hand-reared individual. Calibrates the v4 juvenile's visible age/stage only; does not support a wild nest, population-wide timing or autonomous flight claim.

### PEL-BUTTIKOFER-1889-P115-116
- **Source:** J. Büttikofer, “Zoological Researches in Liberia. Fourth List of Birds,” *Notes from the Leyden Museum* XI, 1889, pp.115–116; https://repository.naturalis.nl/pub/509230/NLM1889011002006.pdf ; read 2026-11-12.
- **Facts:** nestling head uniform white with faint isabelline tinge, especially neck; powerful black bill; maps *S. oustaleti* to *S. peli*.
- **Limit/decision:** isolated head without age/body/posture data; supports only early head-down and bill colour, not v4 body geometry.

### PEL-BRANFIELD-2013-P123-126
- **Source:** Andy Branfield, 2013, *Ornithological Observations* 4:123–126; https://journals.uct.ac.za/index.php/BO/article/download/201/242/688 ; pp.123–126 read 2026-11-12.
- **Facts:** adult shaggy head, poorly developed unbordered facial mask, brown eyes, no ear tufts, black bill/pale base, unfeathered pale legs and riverine forest; large-young call and long dependence context.
- **Limit/decision:** morphology is partly secondary and the paper is a call note; it cannot define a known-age plumage series.

- **Applied:** [v4 research](species/156-scotopelia-peli-v4.md), planned v4 plate and run `owl-pet/production/runs/20261112T183437+0800-cycle-1.md`.
- **Unknowns:** exact wild equivalent of the captive three-month stage, iris chronology, continuous feather sequence, first-flight threshold and population-wide sex ratio. Scientific verification remains false.

## 2026-11-12 — #160 *Tyto inexspectata* v4 — live adult diagnosis and disputed juvenile correction

### MIN-MAURO-DRIJVERS-2000-P180-182
- **Title/authors/year:** “Minahassa Owl *Tyto inexspectata* at Lore Lindu National Park, Sulawesi, Indonesia in December 1998” — Iwein Mauro & Raf Drijvers; 2000; *Forktail* 16: 180–182.
- **URL / actually read:** https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5c1a9e03f407b482a158da87/t/5c1fc4c92b6a282c991dfbbb/1545585868722/Mauro-Owl.pdf ; printed pp.180–182, especially pp.180–181; accessed 2026-11-12.
- **Source type / stage:** primary field observation and sound recording; unsexed adult at c.1,700 m in roadside primary lower-montane forest near Danau Tambing, Lore Lindu; no juvenile.
- **Facts:** adult compact and stocky, smaller than *T. rosenbergii*, with large rounded head, heart disc, black eyes, short yellowish bill, dark golden-brown upperparts, whitish chest, buff sparsely dark-spotted lowerparts, long fully feathered tarsi and strong brownish-grey feet. The observed disc was dark rusty-brown with broad blackish edge; museum specimens can be pale grey.
- **Conflict/design use:** p.181 says Fletcher’s claimed breeding/juvenile record clearly referred to *T. rosenbergii*. Use this source for adult identity; reject the juvenile as species evidence. Disc variation is individual, not sex-coded.
- **Limits/confidence:** high for the living adult and stated conflict; single unsexed adult, no sex ratio, juvenile chronology or nest interior.

### MIN-FLETCHER-1998-P80-81-CONFLICT
- **Title/author/year:** “A breeding record for Minahassa Owl *Tyto inexspectata* from Dumoga-Bone National Park, Sulawesi, Indonesia” — Brian S. Fletcher; 1998; *Forktail* 14: 80–81.
- **URL / actually read:** https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5c1a9e03f407b482a158da87/t/5c1f4f97898583352e27a232/1545555865398/Burton-Kingfisher.pdf ; printed pp.80–81; accessed 2026-11-12.
- **Stage/facts:** an owl interpreted there as a branch-perching juvenile was greyish-white speckled below, browner-winged, calling and scrambling on a high strangler-fig branch.
- **Conflict:** Mauro & Drijvers 2000 p.181 later attribute this description to *T. rosenbergii*. Retain only as a historical correction; it cannot calibrate the #160 juvenile.
- **Limits/confidence:** direct account of the observation but rejected species identity; zero weight for *T. inexspectata* juvenile morphology.

### Reuse and boundary
- Reused MIN-NATURALIS-TYPECAT-2023-P175, MIN-SCHLEGEL-1879-NATURALIS and MIN-COMMONS-GODON-2022-229399656.
- Adults remain near-equal; quantified sex dimorphism is unknown. Juvenile chronology, iris timing, nest interior and flight threshold remain unknown.
- V4 uses an explicit age-unknown down-rich older-young inference with short down-veiled wings, hidden tail and continuous support; no flight claim.
- The user-uploaded Mikkola guide was not mounted; no fresh page claim. Scientific verification remains false.


## 2026-11-12 — #161 *Ketupa blakistoni* v4 — breeding evidence and current insular scope refresh

### BLF-IOC-HAYASHI-2010-BREEDING-ABSTRACT
- **Title/author/year:** “Breeding biology of the endangered Blakiston’s fish owl (*Ketupa blakistoni*) in Japan” — Yuko Hayashi; 25th International Ornithological Congress abstracts; 2010.
- **URL / actually read:** https://ararajuba.org.br/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/Resumos-IOC-2010.pdf ; congress abstract located/read through the indexed PDF; accessed 2026-11-12.
- **Source type / stage:** primary long-term field study abstract based on marked individuals and continuous family observation in Hokkaido, 1987–2007.
- **Facts:** breeding attempts occurred annually; clutch size one or two; females alone incubated 33–38 days; 15 of 16 nestlings fledged at 48–60 days. The study does not say each 50-day nestling could already fly.
- **Design use:** reinforces the documented late-nestling window and female brooding role. Keep the ~50-day bird low at a cavity threshold with support and no flight claim.
- **Limits/confidence:** high for reported summary statistics, but abstract-only and no continuous feather-tract description or individual flight test.

### Reuse and corrections
- Re-read BLF-BIRDRESEARCH-HAYASHI-2010-P1-4: 35–38-day incubation, usual 48–60-day fledging, Photo 2 approximately 50 days, large broadleaf cavities, riverine forest and ice-free water.
- Re-read BLF-CLEMENTS-2026-SPLIT: current *K. blakistoni* is monotypic Hokkaido/insular; continental *K. doerriesi* is separate. Exclude continental white-nape/near-white-tail traits.
- Reused BLF-MOVIN-2022 only for split support. Adult sex plumage is similar; mass ranges overlap, so female is subtly fuller, not mechanically larger.
- Mikkola upload was not mounted; no fresh page claim. Scientific verification remains false.

- **Title / authors / year:** “A New Species of Pygmy-Owl …” / Mark B. Robbins & Steve N. G. Howell / 1995, *Wilson Bulletin* 107(1):1–6.
- **URL / accessed:** https://sora.unm.edu/sites/default/files/journals/wilson/v107n01/p0001-p0006.pdf / 2026-11-13.

- **Facts:** lists a broad Mexican *G. palmarum* specimen series across Sonora, Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco, Colima, Guerrero, Oaxaca and Morelos; notes records to 1500 m in dry pine-oak woodland. The complex context is specimen-based.
- **Limits / design use:** no known-age immature series, nest description or flight threshold. Supports western-Mexico/dry-woodland setting and caution against a universal sex-size claim.

## 2026-11-13 — #173 *Otus madagascariensis* v4 — updated molecular taxonomy conflict

### TSO-MELO-ETAL-2022-P1-54
- **Stable ID:** TSO-MELO-ETAL-2022-P1-54
- **Title:** A new species of scops-owl (Aves, Strigiformes, Strigidae, *Otus*) from Príncipe Island (Gulf of Guinea, Africa) and novel insights into the systematic affinities within *Otus*
- **Authors/institution:** Martim Melo et al.; ZooKeys / participating university and museum institutions
- **Year/type:** 2022; peer-reviewed primary phylogenetic study
- **URL/DOI:** https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9836643/ ; https://doi.org/10.3897/zookeys.1126.87635
- **Accessed/read:** 2026-11-13; full HTML, especially Table 2 and pp./article lines corresponding to discussion of Malagasy taxa (ZooKeys 1126:1–54; Table 2; Discussion around article lines 717–720)
- **Taxa/stage:** *Otus madagascariensis* and *O. rutilus*; taxonomy only, no juvenile-stage evidence
- **Useful facts:** the multilocus dataset includes both Malagasy taxa; the paper reports low divergence within intraspecific range and explicitly retains the conflict between the widely adopted two-species treatment and Fuchs et al. 2007's representative-sampling challenge.
- **Limits/conflict/confidence:** strong peer-reviewed taxonomy evidence, but it does not resolve the checklist choice, adult sex-size direction, juvenile feather sequence or flight threshold. It must not be used to invent plumage/development.
- **Design/check use:** keep the repository's *O. madagascariensis* name while listing *O. rutilus madagascariensis* as an alternate treatment; do not treat taxonomy as a morphology shortcut. Linked to `research/species/173-otus-madagascariensis-v4.md`, `design/concepts/173-otus-madagascariensis-v4.png` and its review record.

## Strix butleri — #223 v1 / current Omani Owl
Accessed2026-11-23. 5 new unique source IDs;1 existing taxonomy boundary reused. Topics: taxonomy/oldnames, adult morphology/softparts, older juvenile/rock support, behaviour/wadi. Each full indexed entry (author/date/type/URL/section/facts/limits/decision) is in [#223 research](species/223-strix-butleri-v1.md#actually-read-new-sources-5-ids-no-third-party-full-pdf-copied-to-repo).
### SBUT-ROBB-2016-REDISCOVERY
Magnus S.Robb et al2016, The rediscovery of Strix butleri..., Avian Research7:7, DOI https://doi.org/10.1186/s40657-016-0043-4 . Original https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40657-016-0043-4 . Read abstract, Methods, Results Morphology Oman/Iran, Taxonomy; Fig2 image actually downloaded and viewed (Oman2Mar2015/Iran23Jan2015). Adults: rounded head/no tufts, orange-yellow iris, green-grey bill, grey disc/dark upper brow and median crown stripe, ginger breast/narrow shaft streaks, white belly, feathered white toes, horn-grey claws. Type/DNA synonym robust. One captured bird measurements cannot establish male/female size direction; illumination changes apparent colour. Supports adult morphology and taxonomy, not young.
### SBUT-KASRAVI-2019-DB-PL233
Ali Kasravi photograph10May2019 Kangan,Bushehr,Iran; WP reports compiled Łukasz Ławicki/Arnoud B.van den Berg, Dutch Birding41(3)2019 p193 plate233, textp198. URL https://www.dutchbirding.nl/journal/pdf/DB_2019_41_3.pdf . Downloaded PDF, actual caption/text read and PDF57 rendered/viewed plus juvenile crop. Primary photo: orange-eyed fluffy pale grey-white young, warm upper chest, sparse grey crown marks, dark folded formed side feathers, feathered feet standing on stone. Not newborn, age/sex unknown. Photo supports represented stage, not exact age, capability of sustained flight or universal juvenile sequence. Lighting may affect grey/buff.
### SBUT-SOUNDAPPROACH-OMANI
Magnus Robb/The Sound Approach, Undiscovered Owls web chapter (book2015; web2019), https://books.soundapproach.co.uk/species/omani-owl/ . Actual text read: opening naming correction, 2013–14 field history, CD4-67/68, WadiMac pair/roost holes, habitat. Old omanensis correctly maps to current butleri. Rocky wadis/sparse Ziziphus, cliff roost holes, juveniles heard begging at600m. No juvenile photograph obtained then; vocal evidence does not describe newborn or prove nest construction. Female warmth/stronger breastband observed in one pair confounded lighting/individual; no generalized sexual plumage rule or size ratio.
### SBUT-DB-2020-P278
Dutch Birding42(4)2020 WP reports p278 (PDF58), https://www.dutchbirding.nl/journal/pdf/DB_2020_42_4.pdf . Downloaded, actual paragraph read: three juvenile Omani Owls photographed Rayan Valley,Kangan,Bushehr5June2020. Confirms another young record; no juvenile plate located on p278, not used as visual reference. No precise age or feather timeline.
### SBUT-TOHIDIFAR-2023-RANGE
Mohammad Tohidifar,Morteza Arianejad,Abolghasem Khaleghizadeh,Taher Ghadirian2023, Major range extensions..., Zoology in the Middle East, DOI https://doi.org/10.1080/09397140.2023.2233774 . Publisher403; author-upload full text actually read at https://www.researchgate.net/publication/372447316_Major_range_extensions_of_two_cryptic_owls_Omani_Owl_Strix_butleri_and_Western_Brown_Fish_Owl_Ketupa_zeylonensis_semenowi_in_Iran_Major_range_extensions_of_two_cryptic_owls_Omani_Owl_Strix_butleri_and . Intro/IBRC records Table1: Kasravi/Nazari Rayan Valley10/30May2019 and5June2020, adult+3young/3juveniles. Same observation as above, NOT independent replication. Their proposed English Golden Owl not adopted automatically. Fish-owl young8Apr2004 belong K.zeylonensis, not this species.

# #233 Bubo milesi v1
Access2026-11-23. Arabian Eagle-Owl, old Bubo africanus milesi. New absent from immutable tree5134f0a2, no alias duplicate. Saudi Tanoumah later juvenile reference.
## Actually read sources
- BMIL-ITIS-1063331: ITIS IOC15.1(2025)/Clements2021, https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?print_version=PRT&search_topic=TSN&search_value=1063331&source=to_print ; Taxonomy/Synonyms/References: valid species; former africanus milesi. High taxonomic confidence, not developmental evidence.
- BMIL-BABBINGTON-2018-TANOUMAH: Jem Babbington, 5October2018, Arbabian Spotted Eagle Owl young - Tanoumah, https://www.birdsofsaudiarabia.com/2018/10/arbabian-spotted-eagle-owl-young.html . Original field account text and first two linked original photos actually read/viewed. July observations: two young, calling, tree to rock flight observed. Young photo yellow eyes, dark bill, short undeveloped tufts, gray-brown/tawny loose head/underbody barred pale/dark, formed folded wing and barred tail. Age and sex unknown; no exact days or newborn inference. Photo reference2 can support a stationary branch/rock stance and retained formed remiges/tail. Colour lighting not calibrated. Original source URL retained; third-party images not republished.
- BMIL-ROBB-2015-SOUND: Magnus Robb & The Sound Approach, Undiscovered Owls species chapter, https://books.soundapproach.co.uk/species/arabian-eagle-owl/ ; sections comparing Tring skins/field observations and adult photograph caption. Actually read: Arabian paler/tawnier/smaller than African spotted; finer speckled/vermiculated crown/mantle, yellow iris/black orbit; wadi woodland and toad hunting. No within-species sex-size measurements; near-equal display is uncertainty-neutral design, not evidence of equal size. Adult photo metadata Oman2013. Exact publishing year chapter inferred from book2015, web copyright2019.
- BMIL-MIKKOLA-2013-P281: HeimoMikkola2013 uploaded secondedition printed281/PDF283 actually read via Library. milesi treated as tawny Arabian subspecies of africanus; general fledgling eye chronology applies broad old species and cannot be assigned to milesi. Photos on page Africa, excluded as milesi identity reference. Reuse shared book, not new bibliography.
## Decisions/unknowns
Adults near-equal height, matching fine tawny cryptic feather patterns; dark bill, yellow iris/black orbital ring; feathered feet kept conservative. Older juvenile based on Saudi actual photos: compact flattened tufts, gray/tawny barred down-like body with formed wings/tail. Supported upright low rock looking slightly upward, no flight scene despite observed flight, no nest. Nest site/materials unknown, not reconstructed. Fine toe geometry/sex dimorphism/precise juvenile age/flight onset and geographic variation unknown. Concept only science=false.
## Iteration hypothesis
Do not apply universal short-wing downball correction to an independently photographed flying juvenile. Compare body fluff and formed remiges separately. Visually validate this output only; no biological approval.

Related image: [233 v1](../design/concepts/233-bubo-milesi-v1.png); [review](reviews/233-bubo-milesi-v1-review.md).

Sandybuff/lightbrown-greyunderparts with limited thin darkshafts/softcrossmarks, no heavyblackladderbars or striking whitescapularstripe. Subtle light scapularareas only. Greybarredfoldedwings, sandy tarsalfeathers down nearlyto grey-browntoes, hornclaws darktips. No copying Socotra short roundedhead or whiteoverboldshoulder.
RIGHT juvenile based on Bates1936p19 and1937p150 Arabian specimens: older feathered juvenile with residual down wisps on feather tips, earthy/dingy general tone and LESS heavy/conspicuous darkshaftstreaks than African Scops same-age birds. Do not depict a newborn or generic cottonball. Soft earthy grey-buff formedcontourfeathers with fine lowcontrast shafts and scattered pale-grey down wisps, a small soft tuft suggestion, compact mostly contour-covered formedwing, no long crisp adultplumes; tailconcealed. Exact young iris/bill/feather chronology UNKNOWN: peacefully rest with headgentlyturnedright and eyes naturally closed, bill mostly tucked into shoulderfeathers. This is a designed restingpose, NOT claimofdevelopmentalclosedeyes. Bothfeet visible gripping a broad low fork, belly lightly supported; no flightaction, no nest/eggs/cavityconstruction.
Environment: southwestern Arabian wadi with acacia-like smallleaves, rocky hills and sparsegreen vegetation, warm muted drywood; not lush rainforest. Adults differing gentlegazes, youngster low settled at naturalfork. Warm soft naturalistic petfriendly proportions, anatomicallycredible, no accessories.

Older immature folded formed wings/developed tufts only, no invented early chick/down/age/flight/nest. Female fuller not fixed taller.
